Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable

Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

vignette: Mateo Reyes stood in the dust-choked compound outside Kandahar when the initial detonation tore through the chain-link fence, sending shrapnel slicing through the canvas supply tents. He had been verifying inventory manifests with three other men when the ground jumped beneath his boots. He remembered the exact weight of the first aid kit in his palms, the acrid bite of cordite, and the sudden silence that followed Sergeant Alvarez's voice cutting off mid-sentence. In the chaos, Mateo had dragged a wounded corpsman into the trench, leaving two of his own men exposed near the breached perimeter. He had been certain that the terrain made retreat impossible, but the mental image of an unlit rifle still resting on the sand refused to fade. When he returned to his apartment in North Carolina, the quiet felt different. He began to notice how the memory of the assault refused to settle into a single story. On some nights, a perfectly clear frame would surface-Alvarez falling backward, the specific pattern of dust on his dog tags-while on other mornings, sudden pieces would appear without warning, like a boot scraping gravel or the clatter of a dropped ammunition box, only to dissolve before he could hold them. He tried to arrange the moments chronologically in a leather journal, but the dates blurred, the sequences refused to line up, and he eventually stopped opening the cover. Over the following months, his days accumulated into a rhythm of quiet retreats. He had come to believe that there was no future waiting for him, that the soldier who shipped out and the man who came back were fundamentally different, and that this difference would follow him indefinitely. He knew he had made a split-second call that prioritized a stranger over his own unit, and he could not forgive himself for acting in ways that went completely against the man he had always tried to be. When he walked past his mother's front yard, he turned down the side street instead. He could not bear the sight of the empty patio chair she kept for him, nor the framed photograph of his cousin Marco hanging in the kitchen, both men taken within a year of each other. He stopped discussing the deployment or its aftermath with anyone. When his sister asked how he was adjusting to civilian life, he told her he was fine, then immediately asked about her job. The habit solidified into something unbreakable. He also began avoiding places where the sky opened up completely. A walk through the downtown plaza felt like standing in the open during an ambush, where everything could be seen and nowhere offered cover. He switched his evening routes to narrow streets, kept his gaze fixed on the pavement, and tightened his shoulders whenever the road widened. As a financial analyst, his days required him to sit in glass-walled conference rooms and review portfolio risk assessments for clients who had suffered devastating losses. He had to attend them. During a quarterly review, when a client began describing how his younger brother had died in the same type of crossfire that had taken Marco and the men at the compound, Mateo's pen snapped against the mahogany table. He realized he could not sit in that exposed room any longer. He requested a transfer to the back-office data modeling team, working in a windowless cubicle where the door stayed shut and the blinds remained drawn. His team lead stopped inviting him to collaborative strategy sessions, and his performance reviews noted declining engagement with client-facing work. What frightened him most was the certainty that he would always be an outsider in his own life, watching from behind a thick glass wall. He came to the clinic because the silence in his cubicle had grown too loud, because he was exhausted from steering every conversation and every route around the things that might fracture him. He did not know how to piece together what had happened, and he did not trust that he could build anything stable again. He hoped, for the first time in two years, that someone might help him find a way to sit through a meeting without counting the exits, or to look at a photograph without turning away.
